data.title: Ketoconazole (topical + oral)
data.body:
_Topicals · I Antifungals — Azoles_

**Class:** Imidazole antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits lanosterol 14-α-demethylase (CYP51) → ergosterol deficiency and toxic sterol build-up → fungistatic
- Strong activity against Malassezia; also mild anti-inflammatory and anti-androgenic effects

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Seborrhoeic dermatitis (face, scalp), dandruff
- Pityriasis versicolor (shampoo as a body wash), Malassezia folliculitis
- Tinea corporis/cruris/pedis, cutaneous candidiasis
- Androgenetic alopecia (adjunct shampoo)

## Dose & formulations
- Cream 2%: once or twice daily for 2–4 weeks (tinea), longer for seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Shampoo 2%: seborrhoeic dermatitis/dandruff — lather, leave 3–5 min, rinse; twice weekly for 2–4 weeks, then weekly to prevent relapse
- Pityriasis versicolor: shampoo on affected skin for 5 min daily for 1–3 days (single-application regimens also used)
- Lotion 2% for scalp/hairy areas

## Adverse effects
- Local irritation, burning, dryness of hair; rare contact dermatitis
- Shampoo may change hair texture or colour (permanent-waved/grey hair)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity (including sulfite allergy for some formulations)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Topical use is safe (negligible absorption).

## Viva points
- Drug of choice topically for seborrhoeic dermatitis and pityriasis versicolor
- Oral ketoconazole is no longer used for skin infections (hepatotoxicity, adrenal suppression) — topical is safe
- Shampoo needs contact time of 3–5 min

## Oral form: Ketoconazole oral
_Imidazole antifungal (oral)_

**Mechanism**
- Inhibits fungal 14-α-demethylase; also inhibits human steroid-synthesising CYP enzymes (17,20-lyase, 11β-hydroxylase) → lowers cortisol and testosterone

**Pharmacokinetics**
- Needs gastric acid for absorption; potent CYP3A4 inhibitor

**Indications**
- Formerly used for dermatophytosis, PV, candidiasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- No longer recommended for skin and nail infections — withdrawn/restricted in Europe and the USA (2013) because of serious liver injury and adrenal suppression
- Still used by endocrinologists for Cushing syndrome (anti-steroidogenic)

**Dose & how to apply**
- 200–400 mg/day (historic dermatology dose)

**Adverse effects**
- Serious hepatotoxicity (including fulminant hepatitis, deaths)
- Adrenal insufficiency; gynaecomastia, reduced libido, oligospermia (anti-androgenic)
- QT prolongation

**Contraindications**
- Liver disease; with CYP3A4 substrates (simvastatin, cisapride, midazolam, ergot)

**Interactions**
- Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (cyclosporine, statins, warfarin); antacids/PPIs reduce absorption

**Pregnancy:** Avoid.

**Viva points**
- Oral ketoconazole is obsolete for skin infections — hepatotoxicity and adrenal suppression
- Topical ketoconazole remains safe and useful

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.42 (Topical antifungals) and ch.51 (Therapeutic shampoos); Khopkar ch.19; Khopkar ch.2; Wolverton 4e ch.10. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._
